title: A motorcycle exam yard in VR, built with Claude Code and Blender scripts: what the AI did and where I had to step in
author: FelipeReigosa
selftext:
This is the newest part of my browser VR project (three.js and WebXR): a motorcycle I can ride and the yard where Brazilians take their motorcycle licence exam. No generated art in it: the AI's part is code.

How the work was split:

\- I modelled the motorcycle in Blender and judged everything in the headset.

\- Claude Code wrote the riding, the sounds and the scripts that built the yard in Blender, driving my open Blender through a socket.

\- The yard was built three times in a day: first from the written rule alone, then traced from an aerial picture, then from the official drawing with its measurements, which is the one I kept. Lesson: give it the drawing, not a description.

\- After that I took the Blender file over. Script-built scenes get you 80% there fast, but kerbs that broke where lanes met, floating roofs and z-fighting were quicker to fix by hand than to describe.

\- The trees are a CC0 low-poly pack. Claude wrote the scripts that plant them, tint each one and export every model once, to be drawn as instances.

\- The sounds are made in code. Since Claude can't hear, it compared spectrograms of a recorded starter and horn with its own until they matched. The starter took three tries.

\- Testing: a WebXR emulator in a background browser tab lets Claude check its own work before I put the headset on. It catches logic, not feel. Everything about feel (the hands on the grips, how the bar steers, getting off) took a round in the headset.

The source is public, together with every conversation it was built in, my prompts and Claude's replies: [https://github.com/felipereigosa/playground](https://github.com/felipereigosa/playground)

Free, runs in a Quest's browser: [https://felipereigosa.com/playground](https://felipereigosa.com/playground)

Questions welcome.

comments.author: WhosLive
comments.body: The spectrogram matching trick for the sounds is really clever, that's a nice way around the model not being able to hear. Your point about giving it the official drawing instead of a description lines up with what usually works best for layout stuff, reference images with real measurements beat prose every time. The WebXR emulator in a background tab is worth calling out more too, since letting the agent verify logic before the headset round usually cuts a lot of wasted iterations. One thing worth trying for the feel side is logging controller and bike state during headset sessions, then feeding that back so it can tune steering curves from actual numbers instead of descriptions. Also really cool that you published the full conversations, that's rare and super useful for people learning this workflow.
